quiz: Most rounds put you face to face with someone. Think about which step happens after the interviews and works from notes.
The interviewer is judging your own contribution. Which letter of STAR is where that contribution shows up?
Look for a bullet that has an action verb, a measured before and after, and the method used.
Recruiters skim each resume for seconds. Think about what length keeps only your best evidence when your career is still short.
Spell out the letters C, A, R, L and compare them with S, T, A, R. What extra step appears?
Several interviewers may ask about the same theme. How many stories per theme do you need so that you never repeat one?
Tracking software reads your resume as text, top to bottom. Which layout leaves nothing it can misread or skip?
Interviewers dig into numbers with follow-up questions. Which choice still holds up when they dig?
Ask who owns the facts on your resume and what AI is actually good at. Which choice keeps both in the right place?
At some companies one interviewer comes from outside the hiring team. Think about why that independence is useful.
People speak about 130 to 150 words per minute. Multiply by two minutes.
Think about what you gain by doing real loops before the one you care about most.
interview: Use a present, past, future structure in 60 to 90 seconds, with one concrete result and why this role fits next.
Focus on what you are moving toward, stay positive about your current employer, and keep it short and honest.
Give two specific reasons that show research: something about the company's product or tech, and a fit with your skills or growth.
Tell a time-boxed story: brief early career, most time on recent roles with a headline result each, then why this role.
Use CARL with a real failure you owned: what happened, how you responded quickly, the result, and the system change you made after.
Pick a professional disagreement, use STAR, show you listened and compared options fairly, and end with a measurable result.
Back the strength with evidence and a number; name a real, non-fatal weakness and the concrete steps you are taking.
Ask about the level and band first, give a researched range for total compensation, and never lie about current pay.
Explain STAR with rough time shares, CARL for failures, using I for your actions, and ending with a measurable result and learning.
Show a method: researching the company, updating your resume, building a story bank, practising, mocks, and honest AI use.
Always have 2 or 3 thoughtful questions about success, challenges, growth or the team, not things answered online.
Pick one number and explain how it was measured: baseline, change made, after measurement, and any honest caveats.
Position AI as an assistant, not an author: what you use it for, verifying output, not inventing facts, and protecting confidential data.
